title: The place
subtitle: Limestone, monks and climats
objectives: Explain the role of the monks

steps.title: A long, narrow region
steps.body: Burgundy, Bourgogne, runs about 230 km from Chablis in the north to the Mâconnais in the south, in eastern France. Its heart is the Côte d'Or, a narrow, east-facing escarpment of limestone and marl. It has about 30,000 hectares of vines, smaller than Bordeaux, but over 1,200 named vineyard sites.

steps.title: Continental and risky
steps.body: Burgundy's climate is continental: cold winters, warm summers and risk at every stage. Spring frost can destroy buds, as in 2016 and 2021. Hail can strip vineyards in minutes. Rain at harvest brings rot. Slopes and east-facing exposure help: they catch morning sun and let cold air drain away.

steps.prompt: Why do Burgundy's best vineyards face east?
options: They catch morning sun and drain cold air
steps.explanation: East-facing slopes warm early and avoid frost pockets.

steps.title: Monks and climats
steps.body: From the 10th century, Benedictine monks of Cluny and Cistercians of Cîteaux studied Burgundy's slopes. They noticed that wines from small plots tasted consistently different and enclosed them with walls, called clos, like Clos de Vougeot. These named plots, the climats, were recognised by UNESCO as World Heritage in 2015.

steps.prompt: Burgundy's climats were recognised by UNESCO in 2015.
steps.explanation: Yes, as a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgundy runs from Chablis to the Mâconnais
Its continental climate brings frost, hail and rot
Monks mapped the climats, now UNESCO-listed
